paraphrase: Arthavāda is a sentence whose purport is praise or blame; it is meaningful by indicating the excellence of what is enjoined or the badness of what is forbidden, which moves a lazy person to act. It supplements an injunction or a prohibition; (in the commentary) it is praise, blame, another's deed or ancient narrative; and 'it is threefold: figurative where it conflicts (with another means of knowledge), restating where (the fact) is already known, and stating a fact where both are absent'.

paraphrase: The verbal suffix expresses bhāvanā. Śābdī bhāvanā is the prompter's operation conducive to a person's activity, expressed by the injunctive (liṅ) element; ārthī bhāvanā is the activity directed to an act, produced by the desire for a purpose. Each expects three things: what is to be brought about, by what means, and how (the procedure) — heaven, the sacrifice, and the subsidiaries such as the prayājas.

paraphrase: A prohibition is a sentence that turns a person away (from an act that brings harm). Where 'not' cannot attach to the injunctive (e.g. 'he shall not look at the rising sun', introduced as 'his vow'; or to avoid an option), it is an exclusion (paryudāsa) instead: a positive resolve not to look, whose fruit is freedom from sin.

paraphrase: 'An injunction proper (apūrva-vidhi) is for what is not at all otherwise obtained; a restrictive injunction (niyama) where something would be obtained only optionally; where it is obtained both there and elsewhere, it is called an exclusive specification (parisaṅkhyā).' E.g. 'five five-nailed animals are to be eaten' excludes the others; parisaṅkhyā is explicit or by implication.

paraphrase: An injunction is the part of the Veda that makes known an unknown purposeful object. It is fourfold: originative (utpatti-vidhi, e.g. 'he offers the Agnihotra'), which conveys only the form of the act; applicatory (viniyoga-vidhi, e.g. 'he offers with curd'), which conveys the relation of subsidiary and principal; performative (prayoga-vidhi), which conveys the promptness of performance; and eligibility (adhikāra-vidhi, e.g. 'one desiring heaven should sacrifice'), which conveys ownership of the fruit.
notes: Checked against the local TeX e-text of the Arthasaṅgraha (section names are this unit's labels; the text has no standard numbering).

paraphrase: The applicatory injunction is assisted by six means: direct statement (śruti), indicative power (liṅga), syntactic connection (vākya), context (prakaraṇa, major and minor), position (sthāna) and name (samākhyā); śruti is threefold (by case-ending, by a common expression, by one word). Subsidiaries are 'proximate helpers' that act on a material (like husking or sprinkling) or 'remote helpers' enjoined by themselves (like the prayājas), which serve only toward the final apūrva.
